title: How Much Does a Credit Pull Cost Lenders
summary: Credit pull costs vary by report type, contract, scores and access route. CFPB cited $18–$30 for single mortgage reports and $40–$60 for tri-merge in 2024.
body_markdown:
Every credit decision starts with data, and that data has a price. For lenders and fintech teams, the first budgeting question is simple: how much does a credit pull cost? This guide breaks down the cost layers, report types and access routes so you can plan spend per decision.


A credit pull is a request for a person's or business's credit report from a credit bureau. The three national consumer bureaus are Equifax, Experian and TransUnion.


‍


### How much does a credit pull cost?


There's no single public price for a credit pull. What a lender pays depends on report type, contract terms, score add-ons and access route—direct bureau contract, reseller or API platform. Pricing typically varies by contract, so published numbers are rare.


The clearest public benchmark comes from mortgage lending. In May 2024[CFPB remarks on credit report costs](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/archive/newsroom/prepared-remarks-of-cfpb-director-rohit-chopra-at-the-mortgage-bankers-association/) , Director Rohit Chopra said: "Single credit reports now typically cost between $18 to $30 for an individual report, $24 to $40 for a joint report, and $40 to $60 for a tri-merge report provided by resellers."


Treat those figures as dated and mortgage-only. A tri-merge report combines files from all three bureaus into one document. These ranges don't price soft pulls, business reports or fintech API calls, and mortgage prices have risen since.


‍


### Why there is no single price for a credit pull


A credit check cost is built from several parts, and most of them are negotiated. Four drivers shape the number on your invoice.


- **Negotiated pricing:** Pricing is typically negotiated, and bureaus generally don't publish rate cards.
- **Report type:** A single-bureau file, a tri-merge report and a business report are typically priced differently.
- **Permissible purpose:** The[FCRA permissible purposes statute](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1681b) requires a permissible purpose to obtain a consumer report. The user must certify that purpose, such as a credit transaction.
- **Contract terms:** Contracts may include setup fees or minimums. These terms can change your effective price per pull.


Under those drivers sit three cost layers. The bureau sets a wholesale price for its data, and a score provider like FICO charges a royalty for each score. A reseller—a company that buys bureau data wholesale and sells it to lenders—adds its own markup.


Mortgage shows how the score layer works. The October 1, 2025[FICO direct license announcement](https://investors.fico.com/news-releases/news-release-details/fico-launches-cost-cutting-direct-license-program-mortgage) said: "Under the new performance model, the royalty fee for the FICO Score will be $4.95 per score."


FICO also listed a $33 funded-loan fee per borrower per score, or a $10 per-score alternative. FICO says it doesn't control the markups bureaus add in their channels. That means a lender's final cost can sit well above the royalty alone.


‍


### Credit pull costs by report type


Each report type serves a different step in the lending flow. Exact prices aren't public for most of them, so the drivers matter more than any single figure.


A soft pull checks credit without affecting the borrower's score, often for prequalification. A hard pull is a full inquiry made when a borrower applies, and it shows on their report. Our guide to[soft vs. hard pulls](https://www.lendflow.com/post/soft-pull-vs-hard-pull) explains when each one happens.


Report type Typical use What drives the price


Soft pull Prequalification, pre-approved offers, account reviews Bureau contract, data requested


Single-bureau hard pull Final underwriting for consumer and small business loans Bureau contract, score add-ons


Tri-merge report Mortgage underwriting Three bureau fees, score royalties, reseller markup


Business credit report Underwriting a company's credit risk Provider, report depth, contract


Scores and add-ons Credit scores and extra data attributes Per-score royalty, number of add-ons per pull


Soft pulls aren't always cheaper. In its 2024 remarks, the CFPB said bureaus and resellers raised mortgage soft-pull prices to match hard pulls. Outside mortgage, soft-pull pricing depends on your contract.


Business credit reports from Dun & Bradstreet, Experian and Equifax cover payment history, public records and business scores—see our breakdown of[business credit report sections](https://www.lendflow.com/post/what-shows-up-on-a-business-credit-report) . They're separate products from consumer reports; pricing isn't published and varies by provider, report depth and contract. Some small business lenders also pull an owner's personal report, which can add a second cost per decision.


‍


### Direct bureau contract vs. reseller vs. API platform


How you buy credit data changes your cost as much as what you buy. Lenders use three main routes, and each trades setup effort against flexibility.


A direct contract means you sign with each bureau yourself. A reseller buys data wholesale and resells it, often bundled. An API platform connects you to several bureaus through one integration.


Factor Direct bureau contract Reseller API platform


Setup May include a separate contract, credentialing and integration per bureau May include one contract; reseller manages bureau relationships May include one integration; may use your credentials or the platform's


Minimums May include volume commitments; varies by contract Varies by contract Varies by contract


Per-pull pricing model Varies by contract and product May include bureau wholesale price plus reseller markup Varies by contract; may be bundled


Bureau coverage One bureau per contract Varies by reseller May cover consumer and business bureaus


Time to launch Varies; each bureau reviews you separately Varies by reseller Varies; may be shorter when connections already exist


Resellers sit between lenders and bureaus. The CFPB has said Equifax, Experian and TransUnion typically set the wholesale price resellers pay, which is then passed on to users. For timelines by approach, see our[credit bureau integration costs](https://www.lendflow.com/post/credit-bureau-integrations) breakdown.


Early-stage lenders face a different trade-off. Lendflow's guide to[accessing credit bureau data](https://www.lendflow.com/post/fintech-startup-credit-bureau-data-access) notes that direct contracts can involve setup costs and minimum monthly pull volumes. At low volume, those terms can outweigh per-pull savings.


Lendflow is one API platform option. Its Credit Engine works with your bureau credentials or Lendflow's.


‍


### How Equifax and other bureau API access is priced


Teams asking "how much does Equifax API access cost?" find the same answer: production pricing isn't published. Testing is free, though, and the path to live access is clear.


Equifax's developer portal uses three stages—sandbox, test and live. The[Equifax developer environments documentation](https://developer.equifax.com/documentation) states: "You don't incur any cost for testing the API in the Sandbox environment."


Moving to test needs Equifax approval, which Equifax says typically takes less than 48 hours. Going live adds another app review. Production APIs only accept calls from whitelisted IP addresses.


For production, Equifax says pricing varies by API product and directs you to an Equifax representative. Production pricing for bureau APIs is generally negotiated, so plan to request a quote.


Sandbox access isn't the same as production approval. The FCRA requires a permissible purpose to obtain a consumer report, and Equifax reviews your app before go-live. Our[credit bureau API guide](https://www.lendflow.com/post/credit-bureau-api) covers credentialing and tri-merge vs. single-bureau pulls.


‍


### Hidden costs beyond the per-pull price


The per-pull price is only part of the bill. Budget by cost per decision—the total data spend to approve or decline one applicant.


- **Credentialing:** Bureaus generally vet new data users before granting production access. Approval can add time and paperwork.
- **Monthly minimums:** Some contracts may include minimum pull volumes. Terms vary by contract.
- **Compliance:** FCRA obligations can add staff time or tooling cost. The scope typically varies by product and use case.
- **Repeat pulls:** A single loan can involve more than one pull. In mortgage, reports can expire before closing.


TransUnion's[credentialing requirements for data reporting customers](https://www.transunion.com/data-reporting/getting-started) show what bureau vetting can involve. It lists "Third party verification of business credentials" among typical items. It adds that an on-site inspection is "generally required if personally identifiable consumer information is being sought."


Repeat pulls are common in mortgage. The[Fannie Mae credit document age](https://selling-guide.fanniemae.com/sel/b1-1-03/allowable-age-credit-documents-and-federal-income-tax-returns) rule says credit documents "must be no more than four months old on the note date." Older reports may need updating, which can mean another pull.


A[CHLA per-loan cost survey](https://www.housingwire.com/articles/fico-tri-merge-price-jump/) (HousingWire, April 2026) found whole-loan credit costs for conventional mortgages rose "from about $50 in 2022 to roughly $540 in 2026." CHLA attributes the increase mainly to FICO price hikes. A FICO spokesperson said charges beyond its fees are "collected by the credit bureaus or other parties but not by FICO."


### Why credit pull prices keep rising


Mortgage credit report costs are still climbing. HousingWire reported in November 2025 that[resellers expect 2026 increases](https://www.housingwire.com/articles/mortgage-credit-report-costs-2026/) : "Credit report prices for mortgage lenders will increase by up to 50% in 2026."


The cause of these increases is disputed, as the CHLA survey coverage above shows. Treat any single explanation with care.


In September 2026, HousingWire covered[FHFA bi-merge consideration](https://www.housingwire.com/articles/fhfa-bi-merge-credit-report-vantagescore-pulte/) , quoting FHFA Director Bill Pulte: "We are seriously considering bi-merge, and stronger solutions (SAFER and SOUNDER)." Bi-merge would use two bureau reports instead of three, but it's only under consideration. Tri-merge reportedly remains standard, and the[Fannie Mae Selling Guide scores](https://selling-guide.fanniemae.com/sel/b3-5.1-01/general-requirements-credit-scores) section still requires lenders to "request credit scores for each borrower from each of the three credit repositories."


‍


### How to lower your cost per credit decision


You can't set bureau prices, but you can control when, how often and from where you pull. These four levers cut wasted spend per decision.


- **Soft pull first:** Use a soft pull to prequalify and route applicants. Save the hard pull for when a borrower accepts an offer.
- **Conditional triggers:** Pull extra data only when a rule calls for it, such as a thin file or borderline score.
- **Decline waterfalls:** Try another source before declining a thin file. Our[credit waterfall strategies](https://www.lendflow.com/post/credit-waterfall) guide shows how to set one up.
- **One API for all bureaus:** Connect consumer and business bureau data through a single integration instead of separate builds.

### Frequently asked questions about credit pull costs


These answers cover the questions lenders and fintech teams ask most when budgeting for credit data. Mortgage figures are dated and don't apply to other loan types.


#### How much does a credit pull cost?


There's no single public price, because cost depends on report type, contract terms, add-ons and access route. In mortgage, the CFPB cited $18 to $30 for a single report and $40 to $60 for a tri-merge in 2024.


#### How much does Equifax API access cost?


Sandbox testing is free, according to Equifax's developer documentation. Production pricing varies by API product and isn't published, so you'll need a quote from an Equifax representative.


#### Is a soft pull cheaper than a hard pull?


Not always—the CFPB said in 2024 that mortgage soft-pull prices were raised to match hard pulls. Outside mortgage, the price gap depends on your bureau or reseller contract.


#### Do lenders pay for business credit reports differently?


Yes—business reports from Dun & Bradstreet, Experian and Equifax are separate products from consumer reports. Their pricing isn't published and varies by provider, report depth and contract.


#### Can a lender charge borrowers a credit report fee?


The CFPB said in 2024 remarks that, in mortgage lending, lenders often recover screening costs through origination fees or interest rates. It also warned that passing screening costs to borrowers can risk violating fee limits.


#### Will bi-merge lower costs?


Bi-merge could cut the bureau reports per mortgage from three to two. FHFA has only said it is considering bi-merge, so no savings are in place yet.
